full_text_en:
HuaMou Technology Co., Ltd. v. WangMou (Beijing) Network Technology Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over infringement of invention patent

Ruling Summary

Where a holder of a standard essential patent initiates a patent infringement liability action against a standard implementer before a Chinese court, and preliminary facts indicate that the holder has fulfilled its FRAND obligations in the licensing negotiations while the implementer has clear fault in the negotiation process, and the implementer applies for an anti-suit (or anti-enforcement) injunction from a foreign court against the Chinese court action, improperly obstructing the holder's legitimate procedural right to advance the case and enforce the judgment in the Chinese court, the holder's application for a counter anti-suit (or counter anti-enforcement) injunction has factual basis and legal grounds and may be granted in accordance with law.

Supreme People's Court
Civil Ruling

(2024) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong No. 914 and No. 915

Applicant: HuaMou Technology Co., Ltd. Address: Longgang District, Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, People's Republic of China.
Legal Representative: Zhao, Manager of the Company.
Agent ad litem: Mao Jin, lawyer of Beijing King & Wood Mallesons Law Firm.
Agent ad litem: Liu Ning, lawyer of Beijing King & Wood Mallesons Law Firm.

Respondent: WangMou (Beijing) Network Technology Co., Ltd. Address: Haidian District, Beijing, People's Republic of China.
Legal Representative: Zhou, Chairman and General Manager of the Company.
Agent ad litem: Zhang Hongbin, lawyer of Beijing Linde Law Firm.

Respondent: WangMou Corporation. Address: San Jose, California, United States of America.
Representative: Cha Moumou CJ. Pu Moumou, Chief Executive Officer of the Company.

During the proceedings of the two cases (hereinafter referred to as "these two cases") on appeal by the appellant HuaMou Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "HuaMou Company") against the appellee WangMou (Beijing) Network Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "WangMou Beijing Company"), and the defendants at first instance Shandong AoMou Commercial and Trading Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "AoMou Company") and Shandong YongMou Information Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as "YongMou Company") concerning disputes over infringement of invention patent rights, the applicant HuaMou Company filed an application for a behavioral preservation order with this Court on December 20, 2024, requesting:
1. That Respondent WangMou Beijing Company, WangMou Corporation, and their affiliates (hereinafter collectively referred to as "the WangMou side") be ordered not to file the following applications with courts, customs, or administrative enforcement authorities in the United States or any other country or region during the pendency of these two cases and after the judgment is rendered: applications prohibiting HuaMou Company and its affiliates (hereinafter collectively referred to as "the HuaMou side") from filing or continuing patent infringement actions in China against the WangMou side concerning the standard essential patents involved in these two cases.
2. That Respondent WangMou side be ordered not to file the following applications with courts, customs, or administrative enforcement authorities in the United States or any other country or region during the pendency of these two cases and after the judgment is rendered: applications prohibiting HuaMou Company from applying for enforcement of judgments rendered by Chinese courts in these two cases.
3. That if the WangMou side has already filed the above applications in the United States or any other country or region, it be ordered to withdraw or suspend such previously filed applications within 24 hours of receiving this behavioral preservation ruling of the Chinese court.
4. That if the Chinese court grants HuaMou Company's application for a behavioral preservation order in these two cases, the WangMou side be ordered not to file any further counter-anti-suit injunction or counter-anti-enforcement injunction applications with courts, customs, or administrative enforcement authorities in the United States or any other country or region against this behavioral preservation ruling of the Chinese court. HuaMou Company has provided security to this Court for the above application.

HuaMou Company states: It is the patentee of invention patent No. 20181153**.9, titled "Method and Device for Transmitting HE-LTF Sequences," and invention patent No. 20181075**.2, titled "Method, Device, and Equipment for Resource Scheduling." Both patents in question are essential patents for implementing the Wi-Fi 6 standard. Since July 2020, HuaMou Company has repeatedly expressed to the WangMou side its willingness to enter into a licensing agreement on fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) terms covering the relevant Wi-Fi standard essential patents, including the two patents in question, and has proactively submitted offers to the WangMou side on multiple occasions. However, the WangMou side has consistently maintained a negative attitude toward the negotiations and has never demonstrated a genuine willingness to enter into a licensing agreement with HuaMou Company to obtain an implementation license. To resolve the negotiation impasse between the parties, HuaMou Company filed standard essential patent infringement actions against the WangMou side and its affiliates in Chinese courts, German courts, and the Unified Patent Court of Europe between February 2022 and July 2024, including the two patent infringement actions filed in Chinese courts in these two cases. In response to HuaMou Company's patent infringement actions, WangMou Corporation filed a civil antitrust lawsuit against HuaMou Company in the United States District Court for the Central District of California on January 30, 2024, alleging that HuaMou Company violated the U.S. Sherman Act by attempting to illegally monopolize the Wi-Fi technology market. During this period, WangMou Corporation informed HuaMou Company that it intended to further file a rate-setting action with the U.S. court, seeking a determination of global licensing rates for HuaMou Company's Wi-Fi standard essential patents. On December 4, 2024, HuaMou Company discovered from publicly available databases of U.S. courts that WangMou Corporation had submitted motions for an anti-suit injunction (ASI) and anti-enforcement injunction (AEI) to the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California. In those motions, WangMou Corporation explicitly requested the U.S. court to prohibit HuaMou Company from seeking or enforcing injunctions obtained through foreign court proceedings, on the grounds that the injunctions sought by HuaMou Company were intended to prohibit WangMou Corporation and its affiliates from continuing to manufacture or sell WangMou Wi-Fi products in the context of the global standard essential patent licensing dispute between the parties. The motions explicitly identified the foreign court proceedings as including the Chinese court actions in these two cases. In response to the above actions by WangMou Corporation, HuaMou Company has already filed applications for counter anti-suit (and anti-enforcement) injunctions with the Munich District Court in Germany and the Unified Patent Court of Europe, requesting those two courts to issue counter injunctions against the motions filed by WangMou Corporation in the United States. Given that the motions filed by WangMou Corporation in the U.S. court cover the litigation of these two cases in the Chinese court and any potential future cessation-of-infringement judgments (i.e., injunctions) that may be rendered by the Chinese court, HuaMou Company has reasonable grounds to believe that WangMou Corporation's anti-suit (and anti-enforcement) injunction motions will prevent HuaMou Company from continuing the litigation in these two cases and will block HuaMou Company from seeking a second-instance judgment from the Chinese court to cease infringement of the two patents in question. If the U.S. court, after a hearing, grants WangMou Corporation's motions and issues an anti-suit or anti-enforcement injunction against HuaMou Company, it will inevitably result in HuaMou Company losing the opportunity to seek legal remedies, including the enforcement of cessation of infringement (injunction), against the WangMou side's willful infringement of the two Chinese patents in question. Therefore, based on the above circumstances, HuaMou Company requests immediate support for its behavioral preservation application.

Upon preliminary examination, this Court finds the following facts:

(I) Litigation status between HuaMou Company and WangMou Beijing Company in China

HuaMou Company filed an action with the Jinan Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province, People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as "Jinan Intermediate People's Court") against WangMou Beijing Company, AoMou Company, and YongMou Company, alleging that the three companies had infringed the two Chinese patents in question. The court accepted the case on April 7, 2022. In these two cases, HuaMou Company sought an order for the above three companies to: 1. immediately cease acts infringing HuaMou Company's patent rights in question, including but not limited to manufacturing, offering for sale, selling, and importing the accused infringing products and using the patented methods; 2. jointly compensate HuaMou Company for reasonable expenses incurred in stopping the infringing acts, in the amount of RMB 1,000,000 per case; and 3. jointly bear the litigation costs of these two cases. After first-instance proceedings, the Jinan Intermediate People's Court found that the accused infringing products offered for sale, sold, and imported by WangMou Corporation, and those offered for sale and sold by AoMou Company and YongMou Company, fell within the scope of protection of the patent rights in question; that in the licensing negotiations, HuaMou Company had fulfilled its fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) obligations; and that WangMou Beijing Company had engaged in obvious delays in negotiations, made unreasonable counteroffers, and failed to actively respond to HuaMou Company's negotiation proposals, thus having clear fault in the licensing negotiation process. The actions of WangMou Beijing Company, AoMou Company, and YongMou Company infringed the patent rights in question. Accordingly, on June 7, 2024, the Jinan Intermediate People's Court rendered civil judgments No. (2022) Lu 01 Zhi Min Chu Nos. 407 and 408, ordering: WangMou Beijing Company to immediately cease acts infringing HuaMou Company's patent rights in question, i.e., immediately cease offering for sale, selling, and importing products infringing the patent rights in question; AoMou Company and YongMou Company to immediately cease acts infringing HuaMou Company's patent rights in question, i.e., immediately cease offering for sale and selling products infringing the patent rights in question; and WangMou Beijing Company to compensate HuaMou Company for reasonable expenses incurred in stopping the infringing acts in the two cases in the amount of RMB 702,278.

WangMou Beijing Company, dissatisfied with the above first-instance judgments, filed an appeal with this Court. This Court accepted the cases on September 3, 2024, under case numbers (2024) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong No. 914 and (2024) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Min Zhong No. 915, which are currently being heard.

(II) Litigation status between HuaMou Company and WangMou Corporation in the United States

On January 30, 2024, WangMou Corporation filed an action in the United States District Court for the Central District of California against the HuaMou side, alleging: monopolization or attempted monopolization of the Wi-Fi technology market; breach of contract for violating FRAND commitments made to the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE); fraud and misrepresentation under California law; and unfair competition in violation of California's Business and Professions Code. WangMou Corporation sought from the U.S. court: treble damages; an order for HuaMou Company to bear attorney fees and expenses related to the litigation; liability for breaching commitments to the IEEE; and a finding of fraud and oppression, with punitive damages.

On November 14, 2024, WangMou Corporation filed an application with the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, requesting to bifurcate its action against HuaMou Company into a rate-setting claim and other claims, and seeking a determination of global licensing rates for HuaMou Company's Wi-Fi patents.

On December 4, 2024, WangMou Corporation filed a motion with the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, requesting the court to issue an injunction with the following content: during the pendency of the litigation between WangMou Corporation and HuaMou Company in that court, prohibit HuaMou Company from seeking or enforcing injunctions in German courts, the Unified Patent Court of Europe, or Chinese courts; and, if for some reason the court does not issue an enforcement injunction for the above request, as an alternative, request the court to set an interim license for the global standard essential patents held by HuaMou Company in the parties' licensing rate dispute. The grounds for WangMou Corporation's motion explicitly mention HuaMou Company's litigation in China and reference the first-instance judgments of the Jinan Intermediate People's Court in these two cases, specifically identifying the dates of those first-instance judgments.

(III) Relationship between WangMou Beijing Company and its affiliated companies

The sole shareholder of WangMou Beijing Company is WangMou International Limited, registered in the Republic of Ireland. The largest shareholder of WangMou International Limited is WangMou Holdings Limited (Ireland). The 2023 annual report of WangMou Corporation discloses that its subsidiaries and affiliates include WangMou Beijing Company, WangMou International Limited, and WangMou Holdings Limited (Ireland).

Opinion of the Court:

The causes of action in these two cases are disputes over infringement of invention patent rights. The core matter of HuaMou Company's behavioral preservation application during the second-instance proceedings is to request this Court to order the WangMou side not to apply to foreign courts, customs, or administrative enforcement authorities for measures requiring HuaMou Company to abandon the ongoing second-instance litigation in these two cases (i.e., to apply for a so-called anti-suit injunction) or to require HuaMou Company not to seek enforcement of cessation-of-infringement judgments obtained from Chinese courts in the future (i.e., to apply for a so-called anti-enforcement injunction). Under Chinese law, such an application falls within the scope of a behavioral preservation application.

Article 103, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the "Civil Procedure Law") provides: "In cases where the enforcement of a judgment may be made difficult or other damage may be caused to a party due to the acts of one party or for other reasons, the people's court may, upon the application of the other party, order the preservation of the party's property, order the party to perform a certain act or prohibit the party from performing a certain act; if the party does not apply, the people's court may also order preservation measures when necessary." Pursuant to Article 7 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Laws to the Examination of Behavioral Preservation Cases in Intellectual Property Disputes, when examining an application for behavioral preservation in an intellectual property dispute, the people's court shall comprehensively consider the following factors: (1) whether the applicant's request has a factual basis and legal grounds, including whether the intellectual property right sought to be protected is stable in validity; (2) whether the failure to take behavioral preservation measures would cause irreparable damage to the applicant's legitimate rights and interests or cause such harm as making the case judgment difficult to enforce; (3) whether the damage caused to the applicant by not taking behavioral preservation measures outweighs the damage caused to the respondent by taking such measures; (4) whether taking behavioral preservation measures would harm the public interest; and (5) other factors that should be considered. Based on the above laws and judicial interpretations, combined with the facts found in the preliminary examination, this Court holds that HuaMou Company's behavioral preservation application should be granted. The specific reasons are as follows:

First, HuaMou Company's behavioral preservation application has a factual basis and legal grounds. HuaMou Company is the patentee of the two patents in question, which are Chinese invention patents granted by the China National Intellectual Property Administration in accordance with the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China. They are currently valid, and the validity of these intellectual property rights is relatively stable. HuaMou Company filed the two patent infringement actions in the Chinese court against WangMou Beijing Company for allegedly infringing the two Chinese patents in question. The Chinese court, i.e., the Jinan Intermediate People's Court, accepted the cases, consistent with Article 29 of the Civil Procedure Law regarding the jurisdiction over tort cases, and also consistent with the internationally recognized principle of territoriality in intellectual property protection. In the first-instance judgments of these two cases, the Jinan Intermediate People's Court found that the accused infringing products offered for sale, sold, and imported by WangMou Corporation fell within the scope of protection of the two patents in question; that HuaMou Company fulfilled its fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) licensing obligations in the licensing negotiations with WangMou Beijing Company; and that WangMou Beijing Company had clear fault in the licensing negotiation process, including delaying negotiations, making unreasonable counteroffers, and failing to actively respond to HuaMou Company's negotiation proposals. The court further ordered WangMou Beijing Company to cease the infringing acts. WangMou Corporation, based on its interest relationship with WangMou Beijing Company, applied to the U.S. court for a so-called anti-suit (and anti-enforcement) injunction targeting the judicial relief procedures, including the two patent infringement actions filed by HuaMou Company in the Jinan Intermediate People's Court, attempting to obstruct HuaMou Company's ongoing litigation in the Chinese court. This application clearly lacks justification.

Second, if behavioral preservation measures are not taken, HuaMou Company's legitimate rights and interests would suffer irreparable damage, or the continuation of these two cases or the enforcement of the judgments would be made difficult. For standard essential patents, the patentee, based on the principle of good faith and the fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) licensing obligations committed during the standard-setting process, generally may not request the alleged infringer to cease implementing the standard essential patent if the alleged infringer has no clear fault. This is explicitly provided in Article 24, paragraph 2 of the Interpretation (II) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Laws in the Adjudication of Patent Infringement Dispute Cases (amended in 2020). However, if the alleged infringer has clear fault in the standard essential patent licensing negotiations, such as delaying negotiations or failing to actively respond to the patentee's negotiation proposals, the patentee still has the right to request the alleged infringer to cease implementing the standard essential patent. As mentioned above, based on the facts found in the first-instance judgments in these two cases, it can be preliminarily concluded that WangMou Beijing Company has clear fault in the licensing negotiations for the standard essential patents in question and is not a good-faith and honest patent implementer, while HuaMou Company has not willfully violated its fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory (FRAND) licensing obligations. Under these circumstances, HuaMou Company's legitimate rights and interests as a good-faith licensor should be fully protected by law. WangMou Corporation's application to the U.S. court for a so-called anti-suit (and anti-enforcement) injunction against the litigation in these two cases, if granted, would at least compel HuaMou Company to consider terminating its litigation in the Chinese court, including abandoning the future application for enforcement of the Chinese court's judgments. HuaMou Company's legitimate rights and interests would clearly suffer irreparable damage.

Third, the damage that HuaMou Company would suffer if behavioral preservation measures are not taken would clearly outweigh the damage that the WangMou side would suffer if such measures are taken. As set forth above, if behavioral preservation measures are not taken, HuaMou Company would clearly suffer damage, including not only substantive rights damage such as long-term infringement of its patents by the WangMou side and inability to obtain timely normal returns, but also improper obstruction of the legitimate procedural rights of HuaMou Company to advance the proceedings in these two cases and to apply for enforcement of the judgments in accordance with Chinese law regarding Chinese patents in Chinese courts. Granting HuaMou Company's application and taking behavioral preservation measures only imposes a procedural non-obligation on the respondent and its affiliates for a certain period, and would not cause any additional loss to the WangMou side.

Fourth, taking behavioral preservation measures in these two cases would not harm the public interest, and this Court has not found any other factors that require special consideration.

In summary, HuaMou Company's behavioral preservation application has factual and legal grounds and should be granted in accordance with law. Pursuant to Article 103, Article 111, and Article 118, paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 7 of the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Laws to the Examination of Behavioral Preservation Cases in Intellectual Property Disputes, and Article 171 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, it is ordered as follows:

1. WangMou (Beijing) Network Technology Co., Ltd., WangMou Company, and their affiliated companies shall not, during the pendency of these two cases and after the judgment is rendered, file any application with courts, customs, or other administrative enforcement authorities in the United States or other countries or regions for the purpose of prohibiting HuaMou Technology Co., Ltd. and its affiliated companies from continuing or initiating new patent infringement lawsuits in China against WangMou (Beijing) Network Technology Co., Ltd., WangMou Company, and their affiliated companies regarding the patents involved in these two cases;

2. WangMou (Beijing) Network Technology Co., Ltd., WangMou Company, and their affiliated companies shall not, during the pendency of these two cases and after the judgment is rendered, file any application with courts, customs, or other administrative enforcement authorities in the United States or other countries or regions for the purpose of prohibiting HuaMou Technology Co., Ltd. from applying for enforcement of the judgments rendered by the people's courts of the People's Republic of China in these two cases;

3. If WangMou (Beijing) Network Technology Co., Ltd., WangMou Company, and their affiliated companies have already filed the above applications with courts, customs, or other administrative enforcement authorities in the United States or other countries or regions, they shall withdraw or suspend such applications within 24 hours after receipt of this order;

4. WangMou (Beijing) Network Technology Co., Ltd., WangMou Company, and their affiliated companies shall not file any adversarial applications against this order with courts, customs, or other administrative enforcement authorities in the United States or other countries or regions.

If this order is violated, from the date of violation, WangMou (Beijing) Network Technology Co., Ltd. and WangMou Company shall be fined RMB 1,000,000 per day, accumulated daily.

The case application fee of RMB 5,000 shall be borne by HuaMou Technology Co., Ltd.

This order shall be executed immediately.

If any party disagrees with this order, it may apply to this court for reconsideration within five days from the date of receipt of the order. Reconsideration shall not suspend the execution of the order.

Presiding Judge: Yu Xiaohan

Judge: Ou Hongwei

Judge: Zhang Jing

December 22, 2024

Judge Assistant: Bin Yuecheng
